questions.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.fact: Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its days are about 430 °C and its nights about −180 °C.

questions.question: How many planets are in our solar system?
questions.fact: The planets in order are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

questions.question: Which planet has the biggest, brightest rings?
questions.fact: Saturn's rings are made of billions of chunks of ice and rock, but in most places they're only about 10 metres thick.

questions.question: What is the name of our galaxy?
questions.fact: The Milky Way contains roughly 100 to 400 billion stars. Its name comes from the milky band of light it makes across the night sky.

questions.question: What is the hottest planet in our solar system?
questions.fact: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, about 465 °C.

questions.question: What is the Sun?
questions.fact: About a million Earths could fit inside the Sun.

questions.question: Which planet is famous for its Great Red Spot?
questions.fact: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm that has been raging for at least 150 years and is bigger than Earth.

questions.question: How long does Earth take to go around the Sun?
questions.fact: It's really about 365 and a quarter days, which is why we add a leap day every four years.

questions.question: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.fact: The sunlight you see left the Sun about 8 minutes ago, so you always see the Sun as it was a few minutes in the past.

questions.question: Which world was called a planet until 2006?
questions.fact: Pluto was reclassified as a "dwarf planet" in 2006. It's smaller than our own Moon.

questions.question: What was the first artificial satellite, launched in 1957?
questions.fact: Sputnik 1 was about the size of a beach ball and sent out a simple "beep beep" radio signal.

questions.question: Who was the first woman in space?
questions.fact: Valentina Tereshkova flew in 1963 and orbited Earth 48 times.

questions.question: Which planet spins on its side?
questions.fact: Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so each pole gets around 42 years of sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.

questions.question: What is a shooting star really?
questions.fact: Most shooting stars are made by pieces of dust no bigger than a grain of sand burning up in the air.

questions.question: What is the huge explosion of a dying star called?
questions.fact: Supernovas spread elements like iron and gold into space. The atoms in your body were made inside stars.

questions.question: What is at the centre of the Milky Way?
questions.fact: The Milky Way's central black hole, Sagittarius A*, is about 4 million times as heavy as the Sun.

questions.question: Which planet is called Earth's twin because of its similar size?
questions.fact: Venus is about the same size as Earth, but its surface is hot enough to melt lead.

questions.question: How many moons does Earth have?
questions.fact: We always see the same side of the Moon, because it spins once for every trip around Earth.

questions.question: What is the largest moon in the solar system?
questions.fact: Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is bigger than the planet Mercury.

questions.question: Which space telescope, launched in 2021, sees in infrared?
questions.fact: The James Webb Telescope has a mirror 6.5 metres wide, made of 18 gold-coated hexagons.

questions.question: Which planet has the shortest year?
questions.fact: A year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days.

questions.question: On which planet is a day longer than its year?
questions.fact: Venus spins so slowly, and backwards, that its day is longer than its year. The Sun rises in the west there.

questions.question: What is a light-year?
questions.fact: A light-year is about 9.5 trillion kilometres, the distance light travels in one year.

questions.question: Which constellation is known as "the Hunter"?
questions.fact: The three stars in a row in Orion are known as Orion's Belt.

questions.question: The "Big Dipper" belongs to which constellation?
questions.fact: The two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's "cup" point the way to the North Star.

questions.question: Which star is the North Star?
questions.fact: Polaris barely moves in the sky because it sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole.

questions.question: What is the brightest star in the night sky?
questions.fact: Sirius is called "the Dog Star". It's about twice as heavy as the Sun and only about 8.6 light-years away.

questions.question: Which planet is called the "Morning Star" or "Evening Star"?
questions.fact: Venus is the brightest planet in our sky, sometimes bright enough to cast shadows on a dark night.

questions.question: What is the name of the American space agency?
questions.fact: NASA was founded in 1958, partly in response to the Soviet Union's Sputnik launch.

questions.question: Which NASA rover landed on Mars in 2021?
questions.fact: Perseverance is collecting rock samples on Mars that future missions hope to bring back to Earth.

questions.question: What was the name of the little helicopter that flew on Mars?
questions.fact: Ingenuity was the first aircraft to fly on another planet. It was planned for five flights and made 72.

questions.question: Which planet has the most known moons?
questions.fact: Saturn has well over 200 known moons, and new ones are still being found.

questions.question: The dark plains on the Moon are called "maria". What does that mean?
questions.fact: Early astronomers thought the dark areas on the Moon were seas. They're actually plains of old, hardened lava.

questions.question: What are comets mostly made of?
questions.fact: Comets are sometimes called "dirty snowballs". Their tails always point away from the Sun.

questions.question: Which famous comet returns about every 76 years?
questions.fact: Halley's Comet was last seen in 1986 and will be back in 2061.

questions.question: Where is the main asteroid belt?
questions.fact: Despite films, the asteroid belt is mostly empty space; spacecraft fly through it without any trouble.

questions.question: What is the Kuiper Belt?
options: A belt of satellites around Earth
A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune
questions.fact: Pluto is one of the biggest objects in the Kuiper Belt, a huge ring of icy leftovers from when the planets formed.

questions.question: Which spacecraft is the farthest human-made object from Earth?
questions.fact: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and carries a golden record with sounds and music from Earth.

questions.question: Which dwarf planet did New Horizons fly past in 2015?
questions.fact: New Horizons discovered a giant heart-shaped plain of ice on Pluto.

questions.question: About how often does the International Space Station circle the Earth?
questions.fact: Astronauts on the ISS see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.

questions.question: Who was the second person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Buzz Aldrin followed Neil Armstrong onto the Moon about 20 minutes later.

questions.question: How many people have walked on the Moon?
questions.fact: All 12 Moon walkers were American astronauts, on six Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972.

questions.question: What is the Sun mostly made of?
questions.fact: The Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of matter into energy every second.

questions.question: What makes Mars look red?
questions.fact: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, which mean "fear" and "dread".

questions.question: Which planet has the fastest winds?
questions.fact: Neptune's winds can reach about 2,000 km/h, faster than the speed of sound on Earth.

questions.question: When the Moon blocks the Sun, it is called a…
questions.fact: During a total solar eclipse the sky goes dark in the middle of the day, and you can see the Sun's glowing outer atmosphere.

questions.question: What happens in a lunar eclipse?
options: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
questions.fact: During a lunar eclipse the Moon often turns red, which is why it's sometimes called a "blood moon".

questions.question: What is the edge of a black hole, from which nothing escapes, called?
questions.fact: The first-ever photo of a black hole was released in 2019.

questions.question: Which big galaxy is our nearest large neighbour?
questions.fact: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away and heading our way. It may merge with the Milky Way in a few billion years.

questions.question: What does the word "astronaut" roughly mean in Greek?
questions.fact: "Astro" means star and "nautes" means sailor in Greek.

questions.question: What are Russian astronauts called?
questions.fact: "Cosmonaut" comes from the Greek "kosmos", meaning universe. China's astronauts are often called "taikonauts".

questions.question: What is the Moon slowly doing?
questions.fact: The Moon moves about 3.8 cm further from Earth every year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

questions.question: Which company's Falcon 9 rocket can land and fly again?
questions.fact: Landing rockets so they can be reused makes going to space much cheaper. SpaceX first landed a Falcon 9 booster in 2015.

questions.question: What is the closest star to the Sun?
questions.fact: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away. With today's spacecraft it would take tens of thousands of years to get there.

questions.question: What is the smallest planet in our solar system?
questions.fact: Mercury is only about 40% wider than our Moon, and it has no moons of its own.

questions.question: When it's summer in Spain, what season is it in Australia?
questions.fact: Christmas in Australia falls in summer, so many Australians celebrate it at the beach.

questions.question: What causes the seasons on Earth?
questions.fact: Earth is tilted about 23.5 degrees. Summer happens when your half of the planet leans towards the Sun.

questions.question: What was the name of the first dog to orbit the Earth?
questions.fact: Laika flew on Sputnik 2 in 1957. Sadly, she did not survive the flight.

questions.question: Which mission famously said "Houston, we've had a problem" and returned safely?
questions.fact: Apollo 13's crew used their lunar module as a "lifeboat" to get safely home after an oxygen tank exploded.

questions.question: Which planet is farthest from the Sun?
questions.fact: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to go round the Sun once.

questions.question: What is a group of billions of stars, gas and dust held together called?
questions.fact: A galaxy can hold hundreds of billions of stars, and there are probably more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches.
